doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Favorite films and jazz documentaries
summary: Crohn lists favorite films, credits Bruce Ricker's Last of the Blue Devils, and describes Altman's Kansas City.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: We’ve got about twenty minutes I would guess, right?
Yeah. Anything you want to talk about yourself?
I want to check my last e-mail is what I want to do.
Do you have favorite films? You know, like “The Godfather.” Those kind of films.
I wish you’d prepared me for this question.
Yeah, I know it’s too hard.

It’s hard to come up with all at once because if I say one film, I’ll forget another film. I mean there are films all over the place. God if I mention some people will say well how come you didn’t mention that one. I mean films like “L’Atalante.”

“L’Atalante” — The Atlantic. It’s about a tug boat. “The Conversation.” I just saw a wonderful film called “Nostalgia for the Light,” a film made in Chile, it was a documentary, “Last of the Blue Devils.” I’ve got to talk about Bruce Ricker because he was the Godfather. He made “Last of the Blue Devils,” and he was a lawyer in Kansas City. And he just was listening to this jazz that he loved and somehow he found some money and got some cameras and he just shot all this stuff and edited the film. Who knew that you could do jazz documentaries in 1974? The only other film before that that was a jazz documentary, there were two jazz films. There was Bert Stern, who was a fashion photographer shooting the Newport Jazz Festival, and there was Gjon Mili films about shooting Lester Young and the dancers and, what’s it called?
Oh yeah. He’s playing and the smoke.
And Sweets Edison. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
And Sweets Edison is in it.

He was a fashion photographer. Gjon Mili, he’s Hungarian. “The Conversation” is a great film. “Whatever Happened to Gilbert Grape,” Leonardo DiCaprio’s first film and as far as I’m concerned by far his best film. And I’m going to not remember — Robert Altman’s “Jazz 34,” which is the outtakes, the outtakes of Kansas City. You know in Kansas City there’s the jazz scene there, but he shot, there’s something called “Kansas City 34.” And it’s a seventy minute film and it starts early in the day, I mean late in the day, like in the afternoon when the musicians are arriving at a club, and it ends the next morning, as the musicians pack up their instruments and go out. And it’s an all-night jam session. And they had Nicholas Payton, David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron.

Cyrus Chestnut, but also the woman piano player, Allen, Geri Allen playing Mary Lou Williams. Each one of them — they didn’t come out and say they were these people but they were modeled on these people. And it was Kansas City the way it used to be but coming back to life. And incredible music. And one thing segued into another thing, there was no talking. I think Harry Belafonte had a little voiceover thing. But it’s an incredible film. I mean it’s not a documentary but it recreated, it could have almost been like a documentary. The minute you walk out of here I’m going to say why didn’t I mention this, mention that.
